sentences.text: The holotype specimen was a subadult individual measuring approximately 70 centimeters in total length, with the tail accounting for roughly 44 centimeters of that span.
This dinosaur displayed unusual body proportions compared to its relatives, featuring a disproportionately large head, elongated hindlimbs, and a shortened neck and forelimbs.
Its hindlimbs were extremely long, possessing a tibia that exceeded the length of the femur, while the forelimbs were very short, measuring less than 30% of the hindlimb length.
Tianyulong is known for a row of long, filamentous integumentary structures covering its back, tail, and neck.
The estimated length of the integumentary structures on the tail was about 60 millimeters, which is seven times the height of a caudal vertebra.
A row of long, filamentous integumentary structures covered its back, tail, and neck.
The skull was especially large relative to its small neck and body.
The filaments on the tail reached about 60 millimeters, seven times the height of a single tail bone.
The genus Tianyulong was first named and described in 2006 by Xiao-Ting Zheng and colleagues after being discovered in Jianchang County, Western Liaoning Province, China.
The genus name Tianyulong refers to the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature, and the species name confuciusi honors Confucius.
A second specimen, IVPP V17090, was described in 2012.
The filamentous structures on Tianyulong are hollow, parallel, and singular without any evidence of branching.
Heterodontosaurids, the group to which Tianyulong belongs, were likely herbivorous or possibly omnivorous.
Tianyulong is classified as a heterodontosaurid, a group of small ornithischian dinosaurs characterized by a slender body, long tail, and enlarged canine-like teeth.
Tianyulong belongs to the class Ornithischia.

Uranium-lead dating of volcanic rocks overlying the fossil horizon suggests Tianyulong lived at least 158.5 million years ago during the Middle Jurassic, specifically at the end of the Jurassic period, approximately 158.5 million years ago during the Kimmeridgian stage, in what is now Asia. Research by Lu et al. in 2010 re-dated the formation to the Late Jurassic, at least 158.5 million years ago. The time range for Tianyulong is from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian, between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
It is debated whether the filamentous structures on Tianyulong are homologous to the proto-feathers found in theropods.
A study in Biology Letters tested the hypothesis that proto-feathers are primitive to dinosaurs and found support for the hypothesis that scales are the primitive trait instead.

If homology is supported, it implies that the common ancestor of saurischians and ornithischians was covered in feather-like structures, and that groups known for skin impressions, like sauropods, were secondarily featherless. If homology is not supported, it suggests that these filamentous dermal structures evolved independently in saurischians, ornithischians, and other archosaurs like pterosaurs.
